utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Hannis, are you ready to resume the examination-in-chief of the witness Mr. Bjelobrk?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour. I believe Mr. Stewart wanted to raise one matter regarding scheduling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It seems appropriate that I should mention this to Your Honours straight away this afternoon, as I indicated to the Prosecution that I would do. I wrote to Mr. Harmon, and also to Mr. Hannis, of course, who is dealing with this witness. It was about an hour ago, actually, a little less than an hour ago, in fact, after I'd reviewed the position, and, well, the way I'd put it then is probably as succinctly as I can put it now to Your Honours. What I said was that I had been reviewing the position on the current witness, that's 651, and the forthcoming, 629, who is a protected witness, and that in particular, I'd been examining the scope and the nature of Mr. Bjelobrk's evidence, including the witness statement, which was incorporated in full in his oral evidence yesterday, and that I had been to see Mr. Krajisnik this morning, as in fact I just interject now, I've been to see him every morning this week. And the conclusion I'd reached was that it was -- I don't make the rulings, of course, Your Honour. Please don't misunderstand me there. But it was my conclusion that it was impracticable and unfair to Mr. Krajisnik for me to proceed with cross-examination of Mr. Bjelobrk at this point. Just going to the end, my concrete proposal, Your Honour, as I mentioned to the Prosecution, and as I put before the Court, my concrete proposal is that Mr. Hannis should complete his evidence in chief of Mr. Bjelobrk today and that we would then adjourn today to enable me to get ready to cross-examine the witness 629 tomorrow, which I should propose to do. And there ought not to be any difficulty about completing the cross-examination of 629. Your Honour, the -- I did mention and I raise this now as well, that the -- there is a broader question here, because the evidence of Mr. Bjelobrk does really raise questions which I've mentioned before recently about the way in which the 89(F) procedure has come to be used. It was originally -- I don't mean Rule 89(F), but the 89(F) procedure which has been developed for the purposes of this trial, as we understand it, it was originally intended to speed up oral evidence by avoiding any extensive waste of time on relatively uncontroversial areas, and at the same time, we worked on a procedure to enable the public, then, to get some feel of what the areas were which were not actually being covered orally so the public could then understand sufficient background to the evidence that was being given. But what seems to have happened, Your Honour, is that over a period, we have drifted into a completely different and, in our submission, inappropriate use of the 89(F) procedure. And generally, Your Honour, the Defence position is that this requires most careful review generally, not right now, this minute, but the most careful review by the parties and the Trial Chamber to ensure that we have the proper and appropriate use of any such procedure for the future. But turning specific to Mr. Bjelobrk's evidence, it's a good illustration of the problem. Your Honour, I would ask just to take a few minutes to run through, very quickly, as quickly as I can, but to run through the statement of Mr. Bjelobrk, which was -- I do have difficulty pronouncing his name, but I don't think I'm the only one that finds it a more than averagely difficult one to pronounce, but I'll do my best. But just the very briefest run-down to indicate what now the really enormous scope of Mr. Bjelobrk's evidence and the enormous potential scope of the areas of cross-examination which it would be, in fairness to Mr. Krajisnik, my obligation to explore with Mr. Bjelobrk to avoid material simply being there as his evidence. Because this has been confirmed as his evidence. This statement is now incorporated in his evidence. And just to run through it very briefly, to start with, Your Honour, the first seven or eight paragraphs are political background, and they're a mixture of fact and opinion. One might take issue with some of that, but I'm not suggesting that that's the problem area. It isn't, although there's rather more stuff there than one would expect. Paragraphs 8 to 12 could be regarded as objectionable in the sense that they contain what -- a great deal of what would normally be regarded as expert evidence. But we try on our side of the case not to be too technical and too difficult about these things. And I also don't suggest that those paragraphs, although there may be some tendentious material in there, I don't suggest that these paragraphs would be the nub of a cross-examination. But we do have quite a big chunk of stuff which goes beyond what he might normally be expected to present to the court. Paragraph 13 is a description of his own party's position. Paragraph 15, then, same as 14. Paragraph 15 talks about the relative party positions and the differences of approach between SDA and HDZ, on one hand, and SDS on the other. And certainly that is an area which needs consideration. Paragraph 16 is a fairly typical type of paragraph in this statement because the single sentence "the national parties wanted to change the borders to change the composition of the population to remove the population and only after that did they want to discuss democracy." There's an awful lot of important stuff wrapped into about 15 or 20 words, though at that point the witness is talking about all three parties, but by definition, therefore, including the SDS. He then goes on in the next paragraph, the SDS, and considers what he describes as local homogenisation as opposed to regionalisation. He makes a comparison with the nationalist movement in Croatia in paragraph 19. If that's of any relevance, that's something that would need to be explored. He draws a distinction between regionalisation and national separatism. Paragraph 20, he talks about an idea which, in his evidence, his assertion, is that came from the top leadership of the SDA. There were many speeches, which he doesn't specify, leaving it to us, therefore, to explore and identify any such speeches for the purpose of cross-examination. He talks about the top of the next page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, the Judges have seen the statement, so it's not a big surprise to me that your analysis of this statement would include the kind of observations you just made, and I think you could go to the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This morning, I prepared a small memo, still to be discussed among the Judges, on the 89(F) procedure. I did that because Ms. Loukas has drawn our attention to the 89(F) procedure already. I would suggest to you that you give us some time to see whether the Judges would come up with a procedure which is amended.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, of course, Your Honour. I'm very pleased to hear that the matter is under active consideration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The matter is certainly under active consideration. So, therefore, I would suggest to you that we do it that way. And I think the Chamber understood what was said by Ms. Loukas. Perhaps, as we did last time, we -- the Chamber then proposed a procedure for 89(F) where the parties did agree, so therefore it was no problem for the Chamber to adopt that procedure. I'm not saying what would have happened if the parties would not have agreed, but at least we could put it to the parties that this is what we have in mind, ask for their brief comments, and then see what to do. So if you'd allow us, and part of it was also that how -- part of my memo deals with the matter of one party informing the other party that certain parts of a statement might not be fit for being introduced in evidence under 89(F), but that viva voce testimony would really be needed for specific parts of the statement. Of course, that could go up to the whole of the statement, but at least that's part of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: At least we'd know that, Your Honour. Yes. May I say, Your Honour, everything Your Honour said so far indicates, with respect, that Your Honour's thinking is going in the same sort of direction as our thinking and our discussions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether that's wishful thinking or reality, I leave that open at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart. So therefore, I suggest that we either even -- perhaps even today, but I don't know whether we'll have sufficient time to do that during the next breaks, but otherwise perhaps tomorrow, that we could deal with the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Tomorrow -- yes, indeed, Your Honour. I sometimes don't even know what day of the week it is. Yes, Your Honour, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I have another question. If you say I better not start the cross-examination of Mr. Bjelobrk today, would that mean that you think that you could start his cross-examination by tomorrow, Mr. Bjelobrk is here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I'm so sorry. I should have made that clear. Because my -- it was -- it was perhaps not made sufficiently clear, but it was implicit in my practical proposal that we should adjourn, I should proceed to deal with the other witness, that that would be tomorrow and that Mr. Bjelobrk -- I acknowledge, Your Honour, I clearly had in mind, although I didn't express it, Mr. Bjelobrk would have to come back on another occasion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, it's a bit of a surprise, after the beginning of this week, where the statement of Mr. Bjelobrk was there, including all the elements that you just mentioned, where he mixes up facts and opinion, where he's not very specific on certain matters, and where the parties have expressed their confidence at that moment that they could finish the witnesses for this week. So, therefore --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: May I comment on that, Your Honour. It's a fair question for Your Honour to ask, but it's a fair question for me then to have the opportunity of answering briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So far as the timetable was concerned, Your Honour, my confidence that we would complete the witnesses was based, if you like, on the arithmetic based on the estimates, which have turned out to be pretty accurate from the Prosecution of how long they would need for each witness and my reasonable confidence that we have generally come within the guidelines on cross-examination. So they didn't in principle seem to be a difficulty. The difficulty isn't so much then the question of the arithmetical timing and so on; the difficulty is to do with the substance of Mr. Bjelobrk's evidence and, Your Honour, there I will frankly acknowledge that noting that Mr. Bjelobrk, A, came into the picture relatively late at all as a witness, and that material from Mr. Bjelobrk has only very recently been available to me, and then, when it did become available to me, what I didn't have available to me, Your Honour, was time to deal with it, because I had so much to do this week. And it's as simple and frank as that, Your Honour. I -- it's only recently that I've had the opportunity, as opposed to taking the opportunity, really, of honing in on specifically what is required in cross-examination of Mr. Bjelobrk and coupled with my discussions with Mr. Krajisnik, of course, to explore what it is. And I can tell Your Honour that it took us an hour this morning for practical purposes to, well, in fact not all that successfully cover one of the points that arises out of what Mr. Bjelobrk says. It sometimes can be a very protracted procedure to get to the bottom of these things. Adding, Your Honour, from a practical point in mind, I just note it in passing as it occurs to me, that when a statement which itself refers to a number of documents is incorporated in a witness's evidence, some thought needs to be given to annexing to the statement at least the more material documents so that it can be read easily without having to scratch together that material. That's a bit of a side-issue in a way, Your Honour, but as it occurs to me, I'll mention it now. But, Your Honour, that is the position. But the substance of the matter is, and, well, Your Honour didn't need me to go through then paragraph by paragraph and page by page, but there are some bigger points still that come up later in Mr. Bjelobrk's statement than the ones that I'd indicated so far when Your Honour said, well, the Trial Chamber has the picture anyway of the scope of Mr. Bjelobrk's evidence. But there are some very big points built into assertions, and of course an assertion made by a witness can be made in one sentence. But to deal with it requires the most careful work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'll refrain from comments at this moment, on your explanation, Mr. Stewart. We'll consider the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'd be grateful if Your Honour has any comments at any point, I'd be grateful for an opportunity then where fair to deal with any such comments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I have not developed them, and if I would develop them, it would be Chamber comments rather than my personal comments. So, therefore, I'll discuss whether your observations are in need of any comment by the Chamber. So would the Defence be ready to start cross-examining Witness 629? I don't know whether that witness is available, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, he's present. I had told victims and witnesses and our investigator handling witness preparations that I didn't anticipate that we would start with him today, but to have him sort of on stand-by for the last hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not in a position to proceed with Witness 629, because what I did do was I have, as I often do, I tried my best up to quite a late stage to see what I could deal with with Mr. Bjelobrk. I do conscientiously make the effort, Your Honour, not to throw away time and not to give up --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say, Mr. Stewart, with a lot of words, you say that --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: A lot of words, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your preparation was such that you're not ready at this moment to proceed with the cross-examination of 629. That's the most important thing I'd like to know because I've got in my mind how to schedule today and tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I see, Your Honour. I was offering a small explanation, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I thought the Trial Chamber might welcome that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think at this moment we should continue the examination-in-chief of Mr. Bjelobrk, and I would like to invite the parties to see whether there would be any way of agreeing on what are the really essential and vital parts of the written statement of Mr. Bjelobrk, that the Prosecution could reconsider whether the whole of the statement, perhaps after discussions with the Defence, would be needed in evidence, and then to see whether we could, with a reduced statement, but it would be possible, after Mr. Stewart would have had an opportunity to speak to Mr. Krajisnik again, to see whether cross-examination could start. I'm just asking the parties to explore the possibilities by perhaps reducing the statement, which would, of course, if it's not in evidence any more, it would need less attention. I do not know. You indicated to us that some part you -- well, there are less important for you to cross-examine the witness on. I do not know exactly what the Prosecution considers to be the most vital parts of the statement of Mr. Bjelobrk. But at least to give it a try to see whether a solution could be reached by, on the one hand, reducing the statement; and on the other hand -- therefore, also reducing the time needed for the preparation of cross-examination. I'm not asking you to answer this question at this very moment. I'm just suggesting it to you. And I'd like to hear from you if that would bring us anything at all, and otherwise, if not, then the Chamber, of course, will have to decide upon your request, Mr. Stewart, to delay and postpone the cross-examination of Mr. Bjelobrk. I do see that Mr. Krajisnik would like to address the Chamber as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I hope Mr. Krajisnik won't mind if I, as his counsel, simply complete first what I've got to say before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I leave it up to you to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- To determine --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- Give the floor to me for the moment, I think, Your Honour. Thank you, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters cannot hear the speaker.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Krajisnik, the interpreters could not hear you, so if it was important, please repeat it with the microphone on. If not, we'll proceed. MR. STEW 1 Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. ART: Well, the tone of voice suggested it was at least positive in some sense. Your Honour, the exercise, in fact, the exercise of identifying some parts is a valuable exercise. I confess, I was also -- I was slightly taken by surprise that the whole statement went in just like that, although to be fair to Mr. Hannis, he didn't tell me it wasn't going to. So I'm not suggesting I was misled in any way. But it's just that if we are -- two points. One is if we are going to engage in an exercise of trying to identify the bits that the Prosecution would wish to go in, it really needs to be done before we proceed any further with the oral examination of the witness, because until we know which bits of the statement are going to be treated as the subject of an 89(F) application and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that if we would continue with the examination-in-chief of the witness, that Mr. Hannis would concentrate on those parts he deems to be of vital importance for the Prosecution case?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. But may I raise a point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I did redact some six or seven paragraphs out of the total of 68 paragraphs, so there was a 10 per cent reduction, at least in terms of numbers of paragraphs, as far as the statement that was introduced through the witness. So it wasn't his entire statement. We did make some deletions before we started.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry. I meant by implication his entire redacted statement and I did at least when I received the redacted statement, for which thank you very much, I did go through and just tick off and check the redactions. But and they were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: They were pretty obvious, actually, most of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the question now is -- the question now is whether we should give the parties an opportunity to discuss my suggestion at this very moment or that we first start -- that we first resume the examination-in-chief of Mr. Bjelobrk and give the parties an opportunity to discuss the matter during the next break. Mr. Hannis, do you have any ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm of two minds, Your Honour, as to which is the most efficient. For one, I planned my direct examination based on the assumption that the redacted statement that was in was going to be his evidence. And then I focused on the parts where I thought I needed clarification of those portions that I presumed would be in evidence. To go forward now, not knowing whether all of that's in or not, I may not cover some things. On the other hand, if I knew from Mr. Stewart what he was concerned about, I might be able to do that. But, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, the other thing I wanted --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The other thing I wanted to add was this, Your Honour, that whatever the outcome of this particular exercise, now for me to cross-examine both these witnesses, and my primary position, Your Honour, is that I find it very difficult, though I suppose waiting until we at least know the outcome of the exercise Your Honour is suggesting, I would reserve a final position, but I find it very difficult at the moment to see how that is going to resolve the position as far as Mr. Bjelobrk is concerned. But if then, in the light of any such discussions, I were to proceed with cross-examination of Mr. Bjelobrk, I wouldn't then be in a position to cross-examine the other witness. So one of these gentlemen would end up leaving The Hague. May I simply say, Your Honour, that I have found on my arrival back in The Hague that the programme of witnesses which was devised for this week, with me taking a telephone call as I passed through the airport last week, telling me that another witness was going to be squeezed in and some brief explanation being given to me, I have found that the programme of witnesses rather heavier than I really might reasonably have understood from those brief telephone calls. Now, that's just perhaps a communication point, but it's a fact. The witness tomorrow is heavier than I had inferred from the discussions reported to me from court and the telephone conversation I've had. So that's where we are, Your Honour. I didn't complain about it earlier this week, because I felt without this particular problem of Mr. Bjelobrk, which has really come very much -- well, which I now see far more clearly, that the other witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: He remains --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand, Mr. Stewart. On the other hand, I think the other witness, Witness 629, was on the motion to have his evidence admitted under 92 bis, that the Prosecution has responded to that. So I take it was more or less aware of what this witness was about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, who was, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't, Your Honour. I was standing in the middle of the airport being told there was a witness from Kljuc. That's all I knew.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, I think it was a witness in the motion for admission of 92 bis evidence on which the Defence responded already prior to next week -- last week.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour, and included was a municipality that was one of those that we were discussing proposed agreed facts on. I don't know what conversation, though, transpired. I don't know what message Ms. Loukas conveyed to Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course. But of course we waited to give a decision until the Defence had had an opportunity to at least briefly discuss that. Let's not at this moment -- I do understand that you're surprised, whether or not this surprise is fully understandable under the circumstances is not a major issue at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, all I was saying is what was devised last week by way of a timetable and reported to me very briefly, all I'll say is it stretched to the very limit, when I discovered what was involved, it stretched to the limit the timetable this week. That's all I'm saying. So it doesn't leave any spare capacity for anything at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There has been taken no decision last week on the scheduling until we received back from Ms. Loukas the result of the consultations she had with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. And I've read those, Your Honour, and they were more or less accurate, more or less accurate, but given the circumstances in which it was done. But I think it was perfectly plain that I was not in a position to know or say very much. I just assumed that those of you here in The Hague, I wasn't far away at the time, actually, but those of you here in The Hague, that a timetable would be devised which was at least manageable. That was the assumption that I made and I'm saying it was just about, at a stretch, manageable if absolutely nothing else was imposed upon it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber prefers to continue the examination-in-chief of Mr. Bjelobrk first, and nevertheless, the parties are invited to discuss the matter, as suggested, during the next break. Mr. Hannis, to the extent possible, would you please keep that in the back of your mind when you resume the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I wills Your Honour, and for scheduling purposes and victims and witnesses arrangements, I would hope that we'll have enough information maybe by the next -- by the second break to advise whether one of those witnesses should go home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Or plan to go home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do hope that we have that information then available. Madam Usher, could you please escort Mr. Bjelobrk into the courtroom. Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I apologise. I had forgotten -- sorry, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik. I have to apologise, because it was just a matter of who comes first and not who will speak. Please proceed, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to thank you. I would just like to assist the Trial Chamber. Your Honours, an important witness is before you today, a very rare witness, especially among the Prosecution witnesses. That's why I have a proposal in this regard. This is a witness who has ideological disagreements with me but who is not inclined to say anything that is not true. In principle, he always tells the truth. In his statement, however, probably because he has forgotten a great many things, he said many things that were quite simply wrong. Now I sound like the witness who was here yesterday. But I have the stenographic notes here that we got from these sessions. If we would show these stenographic notes to the witness, since I know him, I'm sure that he would not say that this is not true or accurate. That is why I would not want to shorten his testimony, and I thank Mr. Stewart, because this shows the very essence of our conflict from before the war. He can confirm a great many things, although we never agreed ideologically. But he will say whether I voted for his proposal or not, whether the Serb MPs walked out or not, whether the session was adjourned or not, whether there were any preparations or not. So I kindly ask you, Your Honours, not to speed things up. We are going to work more productively if we hear this witness out. Not in order to defend Momcilo Krajisnik, but in order to ascertain what the truth is. You will have witnesses from the SDS, but you may say that they are partial. But here you will be able to see two truths, and you will see what it is. This morning, Mr. Stewart, Ms. Cmeric, and I met briefly for an hour. We could not do anything with that hour. There are so many things that are criss-crossed, if I can put it that way. Therefore, I think it would be good for you to hear this witness out, because in the papers you only have the minutes, and that is very short, whereas these are stenographic notes, the actual minutes of every word that was said at the session. I tell you that what he said was not correct, but he is not saying anything that is wrong on purpose. He simply does not remember properly. If you show him the documents, I'm sure that he will corroborate that. So I think that this will help you to understand all the commotion that took place in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I would like to thank my lawyer. I used to be president of the parliament and I would be the one who would give people the floor in order to make it possible for them to speak. So perhaps I transgressed a bit today, but I didn't mean to. I'm sorry. And thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's clear that you underline and you emphasise the importance of fully cross-examining this witness, not only by putting questions to him but also by confronting him with, as you said, the stenographic notes. We'll consider that as well, and I do understand. Have these stenographic notes, have they been available to the Prosecution already? I mean, if -- I do understand that Mr. Krajisnik expects the witness to easily accept if there's any inconsistence between his recollection and what is in the stenographic notes. That, of course, is that matter that might even be solved to some extent already before the testimony of the witness. Has this been presented to the Prosecution before, these notes, or ...? I'm just asking, Mr. Stewart. It should have been through you. The material Mr. Krajisnik is now referring to, stenographic notes of -- I take it of assembly meetings, who voted for what and ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't have read them yet, Your Honour, myself, because apparently they don't exist in English at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. That's clear to me. So that -- well, even sometimes better to present it to the Prosecution so that you have a copy in English as soon as possible. Mr. Krajisnik, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I assist. The Prosecution provided three pages from a certain session. That is what the Prosecution provided. But these are stenographic notes that our investigators got directly from Bosnia-Herzegovina, from the Assembly there. It would be a good thing for the Trial Chamber to have a look at this and the Prosecution as well. Of course, this is not within my rights, but it would be a good thing if my lawyer would first look at this and then everybody else. But it would be a good thing if everybody had a look at this. However, the Prosecution apparently does not have the documents in their entirety. They only provided us with these three pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do not know whether that's true or whether the Prosecution considered only these three pages relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure of what portion of the minutes of the Bosnian-Herzegovinian sessions we have. I know we have minutes of some sessions. As far as the RS Assembly, we have a much greater collection. But prior to the break in October of 1991, I don't think we have a very extensive collection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's not discuss here what is in our files and what is not. I leave up to the parties to include the last remarks by Mr. Krajisnik in their conversations. Madam Usher, could you please escort Mr. Bjelobrk into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Good afternoon, Mr. Bjelobrk.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon to all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I first apologise that you had to wait such a long time. We had a procedural issue we had to discuss first, and it took the time it took. Mr. Hannis, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we notice the witness did bring some materials with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Bjelobrk, I can't see what is on your desk because it's all hidden through your monitor. Could I invite you, whenever you have any material there, to keep it away. If you want to consult it or if you feel any need to consult it, please indicate so and tell us what you'd like to consult and then we'll decide on whether it's appropriate or not for you to consult any notes or papers. Please proceed, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: For the record, it appeared that on top he had a copy of his witness statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Hannis: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelobrk, when we stopped yesterday I was asking you about paragraph 22 of your statement, where you talked about --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, for the record, Your Honour, it was quite clear he's got more than a copy of his witness statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, it's closed. It's not there anymore although I see still one piece of paper which seems to be open. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were describing an event that happened in the Assembly in which your party was trying to get a matter on the agenda. Just -- if you could clarify it for me a little bit about how it worked in the Bosnia-Herzegovina Assembly in 1991. First of all, approximately how many deputies or members were there in the entire Assembly? Do you know that number?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, I'll speak to the best of my recollection, but I don't think I'll make any major mistakes. There were about 240 MPs, about 80 per cent were the deputies of the three national parties, and the rest were the opposition parties, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And for a piece of legislation or a decision to be reached by the Assembly, what percentage of the members had to agree?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a majority system, so there had to be a simple majority of 51 per cent. There was a few special issues which required a different kind of majority, but as far as procedural issues were concerned, like the adoption of the agenda and other matters, that was voted on by simple majority.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there were, as I understand it, two separate bodies within the Assembly. Can you tell us what those were and what the difference was between those two?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were two chambers, something that may be reminiscent of a lower and an upper house. There was the Chamber of Citizens and a Chamber of Municipalities. A deputy in the Chamber of Citizens would come from party lists. As far as the Chamber of Nationalities was concerned, there were direct candidatures of specific names and surnames and they had the backing of individual political parties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as for the Chamber of Municipalities?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Chamber of Municipalities had 105 deputies, I think. It corresponded to the number of municipalities in Bosnia-Herzegovina and from every municipality there was one deputy. Similar agendas were discussed at both chambers. For a certain number of issues, they were mainly discussed by the Chamber of Citizens. But there were many issues that were discussed by both chambers. Also, as far as major debates are Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. concerned, there was the possibility of having what was called joint sessions of both chambers of the Assembly, and that did happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, there seems to be -- Ms. Cmeric tells me there's an interpretation issue. Chamber of Nationalities, where that appears, page 22, line 9, that, according to Ms. Cmeric, that was Chamber of Municipalities in the answer. I think through Mr. Hannis, not surprisingly, as probably others, because we end up in fact with the wrong number of chambers if such a body existed, the Chamber of Nationalities.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note that the witness used the expression "Vijece Naroda" only once, which would be Chamber of Nationalities, and that was referred to only once.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelobrk, just to be clear: There were only two chambers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Chamber of Citizens and the Chamber of Municipalities?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 25 of your statement, and if you need to refer to it, we can have Exhibit 392 handed to you if you need to check something I'm asking you about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, have you left paragraph 22 or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. You go back. You're not finished. Okay. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I'll start my question now while the statement's on its way to you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you describe a pre-parliamentary procedure, and you talk about the Collegium of the Assembly. Can you explain to me a little bit about how that worked? First of all, what was the Collegium?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Collegium was basically a consultative body of the president to the parliament and consisted of the president, vice-president of the parliament and also the heads of the clubs of the members of the parliament. If there were three members coming from particular parties, they constituted a club and they were supposed to reach organisational agreements on organisational matters, although often efforts were made to reach political agreements within such a small framework. So part of the atmosphere of obstruction that I talked about yesterday was basically formulated in that Collegium, although later on the three national parties agreed that once the agenda is adopted, there has to be agreement among the heads of clubs of these three parties, and the others were not even asked. Although each and every member of parliament could propose a particular item to be included on the agenda, in case it was not included already and if they wanted to have it discussed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in addition to the three national parties, how many other parties in the BH Assembly at that time were of sufficient size to have a Deputies Club and a member of the Collegium?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now I'm really speaking from memory only. I think there were three or four parties. It was the SDP, the reformists. I'm not sure whether the Liberal Party had a club of deputies. And that would be about it. Again, I'm speaking from memory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to go back for a moment to paragraph 22, and yesterday you told us that the particular item that your party was trying to get on the agenda related to this principle of the equidistant position of Bosnia vis-a-vis Croatia on the one hand and Serbia on the other; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Until the summer of 1991, there was a series of talks that took place among the presidents of the republics. Our proposal to the parliament was motivated by the failure of the split meeting of the presidents of the republics. We wanted to offer a solution which would lead to compromise and to a democratic denouement. We proposed a set of positions which would define the stand of Bosnia-Herzegovina in these negotiations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the first step in getting something like that passed by the Assembly was to get on the agenda; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. The formal sponsor of the proposal for an agenda of an Assembly meeting is the president of the Assembly. That is in accordance with the rules of procedure. So the president of the Assembly has to receive such proposals first. So we presented our proposal to have this kind of material be placed on the agenda of the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And once it's presented to the president, what happens next? Is it simply up to him or is it voted on by a larger group or how does that work?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. He is the official proposing party, and the members of parliament vote on the proposal. In the meantime, it can be amended through interventions of other MPs. So ultimately, the president of the parliament does have the right to put forth proposals, but all MPs would have the same right while the session was still in the opening stage. So this was a proposal of the SDP, and the proposal was accepted by the president then. And it was discussed. However, when the debate started on whether it would be supported by the MPs or not, then we came across hurdles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What hurdles did you come across? What happened?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this polemic, to put it briefly, whether this proposal of ours would be debated within the agenda or not, the MPs of the SDS left the session after a protracted debate and a very unpleasant one, in my opinion. Mr. Krajisnik stayed on and chaired the session, and he also voted in favour of putting this proposal on the agenda, as opposed to all the other SDS MPs. When it was finally debated, there was almost a quorum. The number of persons present was equal to a quorum. All the MPs who were present at that moment were of the number that was required for adopting the proposal. However, finally, Mr. Krajisnik was the only one to vote against it, whereas all the other MPs voted for the proposal. It was very unpleasant, if I can put it that way, for a simple reason. If it is a political demonstration staged by the SDS MPs when they walked out, Mr. Krajisnik did stay on. On the other hand, it was natural that we expected to have a democratic discussion of different views on this. However, he knew that he was the one remaining vote that could tip the scales, and that did happen ultimately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you a few questions on this item 22. In your statement, and also in your testimony, you tell us how Mr. Krajisnik obstructed. A few questions. Do you consider Mr. Krajisnik not leaving the Assembly, but staying, to be an act of obstruction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I do not. As a deputy, he performed his duties as president of the Assembly in a very correct manner. He maintained the order of the Assembly, abided by the agenda, the rules of procedure, et cetera. However --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you. Next question: In your opinion, should Mr. Krajisnik have voted against adopting this item on the agenda?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the position of all the MPs from that club was that, then it was only natural that he would disagree like the rest. The fact that he stayed behind means that it was manipulation. That's the way I see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If he would have blocked adopting this issue on the agenda, would you have considered this a contribution to the democratic process in the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Had he blocked it, I would not have considered that to be a contribution to a democratic process, because I do not think that stopping a democratic debate can be considered an act of democracy. It is quite illogical. He is primus inter pares within the Assembly but he is a member of the club of deputies of the SDS and they define their position by walking out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The next question is: Would you have expected Mr. Krajisnik, who was an SDS member, to have voted in favour of a proposal which the SDS opposed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not expect that, not at any moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you considered the possibility that the responsibility of Mr. Krajisnik, as speaker of the Assembly, could have taken the view that it would not have been appropriate for him to block something to be put on the agenda, thus preventing it from further being discussed in the Assembly; and at the same time, as an SDS member, that it was appropriate for him not to vote in favour after the discussions had taken place in the Assembly, on the matter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I've understood you correctly, as I see a democratic procedure, every president of an assembly, an MP, should allow a democratic debate to take place. And of course, it is natural that at the end of a debate, every MP should vote in favour or against a proposal, depending on his stance. This was a manipulation in terms of whether something should be put on the agenda or not, because the political affiliates of Mr. Krajisnik left the session, at the time when a decision was to be taken about the agenda.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would the outcome have been any different if they would have stayed and voted against it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am certain that it would not have been different. That's not the point. But at least we would have had a democratic debate, we would have spoken our minds, and we would have heard different opinions, probably, and taken a step further. But when you're leaving a place where democratic decisions are to be taken, then there's no further step to be taken at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand your view as well if you say that you would have appreciated to hear the positions of those members that had left the Assembly as a contribution to the democratic debate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, because the general public, the community, would be hearing everyone's opinions and all the MPs would have something to take into consideration while discussing the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you considered leaving the Assembly meeting by the SDS Assembly members as manipulative for the democratic debate; is that a proper understanding of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, above all, what president of the Assembly did was manipulative, because he was there in two capacities, because he was president of the Assembly, proceeding under the statutes of the Assembly, but, like all of his other colleagues from the SDS club, he was an SDS deputy, so he was there wearing two hats, basically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But do you mean to say that they should have left or should have stayed, with the others, or should they have left with the others or should they have stayed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All of them should have stayed and taken part in the debate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that you blame the other representatives for leaving the Assembly meeting. My next question would be: Could Mr. Krajisnik have made them to stay? Did he have any power? Did he have any competence to prevent them from leaving?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as some special competences are concerned, in terms of the internal rules within a deputies club, I don't think there are any such special competences or authorities that any one of them could have vis-a-vis the others. But I'm starting from first of all the authority of the president of the Assembly, on the one hand, and on the other, authority of some of the SDS leaders. I would hold them responsible and think that they should have held themselves responsible in terms of securing that a democratic debate does take place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any fact known to you which would demonstrate that Mr. Krajisnik was encouraging any of the SDS members to leave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know anything about that, because the meetings within the clubs were usually behind closed doors, and I don't know what went on there. But there are other facts to corroborate what I've just said. The general public commented on these frequent intervals during the Assembly session, also in a witty fashion, saying that it seems that the entire Assembly was made up of intervals. The intervals were an instrument to slow down the proceedings of the Assembly, on the one hand, and to introduce -- raise new issues that would help complicate the situation further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: These are comments of a rather general nature. I'd like to focus first on the example, and, if needed, we could go into other areas. Do I understand you well that you say the SDS members should have stayed in the Assembly meeting because their contribution to the democratic debate was needed for a proper exercise of the democratic functions? That's the first element. Do I also understand your testimony correctly if I say Mr. Krajisnik had no powers to prevent the other SDS representatives from leaving? Until now, is this a correct understanding? I'll continue with the next section after you have responded to this question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, you've understood me correctly. And second, I am not aware of any special powers by Mr. Krajisnik, other than those inherent in the function of a president of an assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand from the whole of your answers that you would have expected Mr. Krajisnik to use his influence in order to prevent the SDS representatives from leaving? Is that what you expected from him at that moment? Is that what you thought would be a wise step to take by a speaker of the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, that's what we expected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In paragraph 22, you're talking about an example of the exercise of his authority, and you described that in terms of obstruction. Do I understand you well that the obstruction demonstrated here by Mr. Krajisnik consisted of not taking, as you thought it would be, the wise position to encourage the SDS representatives to stay in the Assembly meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Mr. Bjelobrk, I would -- well, Your Honours, next I would like to play an intercepted conversation for Mr. Bjelobrk. If this could be given the next exhibit number. This is a conversation dated 28th of June, 1991, and this is one that Mr. Bjelobrk listened to in preparation for his testimony today. Your Honour, I intend to play three separate segments within this entire conversation. And for the translators, the first segment begins on page 1 of the English, in the second box from the bottom of the page, where Mr. Karadzic is speaking. And in the B/C/S, it begins on page 1, approximately halfway down. It's the first big block, where Mr. Karadzic is speaking. This first segment, Your Honour, will last about a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do we have numbers already -- have they been played before or is this the first time?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is the first time, Your Honour. I would propose to give the entire tape one number and I'm just going to play these portions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What we'll do, then, is -- you say the tape -- you received that in the form of a CD-ROM or ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So the CD-ROM would have a number and the different parts would get that same number but A, B, and C added for each part. And then the translation would be the number A.1 or the number and then B.1 for the translation into English.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Just for the record, before I start to number, I just want to be clear. You have just this --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: There should be an English and a B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the English, I guess, would be B.1, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's the translation. A.1 would be the B/C/S original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the overall number for the CD-ROM?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The overall number would be 3 -- P395.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So the first part to be played would be P395A, and A.1 for the English translation. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Radovan KARADZIC: No, last night we -- we went out of the parliament yesterday, we won a great victory yesterday, indeed. What our representatives did yesterday regarding the issues of Yugoslavia, constitutionality, laws, it was -- SDA was speechless, barely three of their representatives spoke. HDZ had to legitimise itself to, to ask for the recognition of Slovenia and Croatia and such nonsense. We were leading the game and all of a sudden this fax came in, informing about him -- he is a mad man, indeed. Slobodan MILOSEVIC: Okay, but you should say it doesn't mean a thing, and -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Radovan KARADZIC: No. We said it was in case of breakup of the constitutional system. As long as there is a constitution we will respect it and we will be the last ones to violate it. Slobodan MILOSEVIC: Yes, yes. Radovan KARADZIC: So that was how we carried out that thing, although I think -- Slobodan MILOSEVIC: And why did you break up? Radovan KARADZIC: Well, we broke up because the coalition was trying to impose their things. They didn't want to declare themselves about Slovenia and Croatia. Krajisnik set them such a trap that no matter how they voted, it didn't suit them. If they condemned it, they would have difficulties with their coalition, and if they didn't condemn it, they would encounter problems because they didn't condemn IT. And Izetbegovic came up with six promotes very cunningly, and in the first two he put that it should be accepted although it was a bit too simple. He's a lawyer, a lawyer who said it was simple, but still legal. Slobodan MILOSEVIC: Yes. Radovan KARADZIC: And then our representatives got on the platform and his proposals were defeated. They lost to one vote. He lost to one vote. Slobodan MILOSEVIC: It's strange. It means that not only our representatives voted, but also others. Radovan KARADZIC:. Yes, yes. The reformists voted, they abstained. But no Krajisnik set it very wisely in accordance with the question -- in accordance with how the proposal is formulated. If it's formulated as yes, then he needs 121.0."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelobrk, can you tell us if this relates to the event you were talking about or another occasion?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this refers to that particular event in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know what time you want to break. I have two more clips to play. One is about two minutes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Usually we have a break after one hour and a half, which would bring us to a quarter to 4.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think I can do the next two. Thank you. I would like to play the next one, and before we start, I'll tell the interpreters that that begins -- the English begins on page 3 of the English translation, and it's the eighth block down. And the B/C/S begins on page 3, and it's the sixth block down. I'm sorry. I misspoke. Page 3, the sixth block down and we have Mr. Karadzic speaking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's grey in our copy, so that saves us from counting. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Radovan KARADZIC: Markovic's moratorium didn't pass here last night. If we stayed longer maybe it would have passed but I wasn't sure whether it was good or not. Slobodan MILOSEVIC: Yes. Radovan KARADZIC: Well, we left earlier because of our things and because they didn't declare themselves so we left the reformists alone and then the reformists got mad and they left too, so only SDA and HDZ stayed. The communists left early this morning, they left early in the morning yesterday and now we have weakened the coalition in such a way that they are self-sufficient now. Slobodan MILOSEVIC: They can't sit now. Radovan KARADZIC: Yes. No, no. Not now. It's not possible. Now we are going to dictate whether we are going to go back to the parliament or the. Slobodan MILOSEVIC: Yes, yes. Radovan KARADZIC: And Krajisnik made himself clear, nobody can -- it was -- he was the hero of the day in Bosnia. It was on TV. He literally held the parliament in his hands. Slobodan MILOSEVIC: Yes, yes. Perfect. Fuck the country which doesn't have Bosnia. Radovan KARADZIC: Yes, yes. The country can't go without Bosnia. No way. Slobodan MILOSEVIC: [Laughter] Radovan KARADZIC: We are not going to let it happen."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters correction from the booth. "A country cannot do without Bosnia" would be a more appropriate translation of the penultimate sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if the Defence has no dispute with that, I have no dispute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, suggested in the translation by the interpreters, country could -- "cannot do without Bosnia" rather than "cannot go without Bosnia."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, we agree, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then please proceed, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelobrk, can you tell us, if you know, what Mr. Markovic's moratorium was?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall what moratorium they're talking about here, which Markovic's moratorium.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The last segment I want to play, the English begins on page 6 and the B/C/S is also on page 6, and this one is about a minute, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Slobodan MILOSEVIC: What about Durakovic's men. Radovan KARADZIC: Well, they are desperate. Slobodan MILOSEVIC: Did they vote for the Izetbegovic's proposals? Radovan KARADZIC: No, they left yesterday morning. Slobodan MILOSEVIC: Yes. Radovan KARADZIC: Because they wanted to impose a resolution on the indivisibility of Bosnia. Slobodan MILOSEVIC: Yes. Radovan KARADZIC: It's an context completely, there's no context in it at all. Slobodan MILOSEVIC: Yes, yes, they wanted to collect a couple of points but his timing was bad. Radovan KARADZIC: Yes, yes, they wanted to, indeed, but we played an extraordinary game and Krajisnik suspended the session and he said that the smallest club of two representatives was important to him and that he would not work if -- the parliament had to decide whether to continue without one party. Slobodan MILOSEVIC: Yes, yes. Radovan KARADZIC: That way, we are buying ourselves the right to -- when we leave, the session will have to be suspended. Slobodan MILOSEVIC: Yes, yes. utterances.text: Mr. Bjelobrk, can you tell us who Durakovic was that's referred to there?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelobrk, now I want to go to paragraphs 26 and 27 of your statement, where you describe the SDS as engaging in a "parallel process" and the formation of parallel structures. Can you tell the Court what evidence, if any, did you see or hear or become aware of in 1991 and early 1992 about the SDS engaging in that process, and give us some examples, if you have some.

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that there were three stages in terms of this separation of government conducted by the SDS. In the first stage, the beginning of 1991, the assemblies where the SDS was in power were made bigger.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction. Not assemblies, but municipalities.

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Also, local officials were instructed to implement the constitution of Yugoslavia, not the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The second stage was the establishment of Serb autonomous provinces, which was already an anticonstitutional act, because no such thing was stipulated in the constitution. The third part of this organisation, or rather, the third stage, was the establishment of the Serb Assembly, and that was a directly anticonstitutional act. In the decision on the establishment of this Assembly, there is a provision stating that the Assembly has a legislative nature. I should like to remind you that according to the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina, legislative authority is vested only in the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is why I am saying that this meant the restructuring of government, of state bodies, by introducing this parallel authority, parallel government, in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I would like to have the next CD marked and given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, that would be number --?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be number P397.

utterances.text: Your Honours, I only have one clip from this intercept and it's about 35 seconds long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That would then be P397A for the transcript in B/C/S, and P397A.1 for the English translation. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And for the interpreters, this begins at the very beginning of the translation. I'm sorry, Your Honour. I'm not hearing anything.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Radovan KARADZIC: -- Meet every morning and have it sorted out. I was with Izetbegovic and Zulfikarpasic last night and I told them openly we would form a parallel government, we would form a parallel police, if they exclude our people and government, and they will still have to pay for them. We would exclude all our people who are armed, we would form completely a parallel state, if you continue to fuck around. And he only stared at me, and winked, because he knew that we would do it. God could not stop us in that, because they started to fuck around with us. And there is no doubt there. We would do it in a week. So let the war be. So we'll have it finished once."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelobrk, you told us just before we played this about the three phases that you saw of this parallel process, and one of them that you talked about the municipalities where the SDS was in power were made bigger. How were they made bigger? What did you mean by that exactly?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not made bigger physically. They were instructed as follows: Whenever they're supposed to resolve a problem, they should resort to the provisions of the constitution of Yugoslavia rather than the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is what the situation was in January 1991, if I remember correctly. In my opinion, this was the second stage, in the month of July, and this atmosphere permeated the public, because these were words that had already become recognisable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in the intercept that we just heard played and was dated, I believe, the 13th of August, 1991, did you see any evidence of the Serbs forming parallel governments?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 13th of August? I'm sorry, but the transcript I have before me is dated the 8th of July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I was reading ahead, Mr. Bjelobrk. You're correct. By that time, had you seen or become aware of any parallel structures being set up by the SDS within Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. The deputies of the SDS spoke in the Assembly and they appeared in the media, the officials of the SDS did, and we found out about all of this, about this sequence of events that was unfolding in the municipalities where the SDS was in power. In the summer of 1991, in the couloir at the Assembly, we had the opportunity of hearing what individual SDS deputies were saying, namely that they intended to establish a government of their own.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to have the next CD marked as an exhibit, given a number, please. And I only have one segment in this one.

utterances.text: Yes. But I think we have a CD, which bears the number 398. Then we have the transcript, the original transcript, 398A, and then P398A.1 for the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I'll begin on page 1 of both the B/C/S and the English, and it's about five lines down.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters can hear the same tape that was played before.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS

At the government level. It was -- Nikola KOLJEVIC: Did the Assembly adopt it too? Radovan KARADZIC: No, no. The Assembly is the Board of Citizens. The Board of Municipalities rejected it earlier and whatever the Board of Citizens does now, it would not be valid. No one has the right to do that and nobody will. It has not been adopted and our municipalities will not obey it. They report to Doko on a regular basis. Nikola KOLJEVIC: Has it been adopted at the Assembly? Radovan KARADZIC: No, it hasn't. Nikola KOLJEVIC: Okay. That's the most important. Radovan KARADZIC: No, it hasn't. And also, our municipalities are not acting according to it. Nikola KOLJEVIC: Okay, then. Radovan KARADZIC: Doko is sending, he is sending to, Doko and Pelivan are sending together. Nikola KOLJEVIC: Yes. Radovan KARADZIC: However, our municipalities regularly report that they will obey only the federal law. Nikola KOLJEVIC: Yes. Radovan KARADZIC: To tell you the truth, I did not watch all of that, but the journalist told me what happened. He told me what Kljuic was saying. They intend to create a crisis in Bosnia and Herzegovina. They are threatening to leave the Assembly and the coalition and to join the opposition. Nikola KOLJEVIC: Who is threatening by leaving the Assembly? Radovan KARADZIC: Or the coalition. Kljuic is. Nikola KOLJEVIC: Yes. Radovan KARADZIC: And by joining the opposition. Nikola KOLJEVIC: He would be in the opposition? Radovan KARADZIC: Yes. Nikola KOLJEVIC: Did you continue the talks with Alija? Radovan KARADZIC: Yes, we did. Nikola KOLJEVIC: Was there anything new? Radovan KARADZIC: You know, we both talked, but basically, I said -- were you there when I said that we found ourselves in the situation -- what Alija described is the conflict of two political wills. We are in the situation to decide is there one solution for Bosnia-Herzegovina, i.e., something that would be acceptable for all three nations. Nikola KOLJEVIC: Yes. Radovan KARADZIC: If not, then we should find solution for each nation separately, to find out what would be the solution that every nation can accept, i.e., every nation shall look for its own solution. Because if there won't be any acceptable solution for us at the level of Bosnia and Herzegovina, we will find our own solution. But Momo took a dig at them in terms of referendum. Nikola KOLJEVIC: Is that so? Radovan KARADZIC: He told him: Let's suppose that we get a result. We can guess what the result will be. What will you do with that result? He stopped, as to say: We know it too. He then said: The result will be to our benefit. We will have the benefit of the referendum results. Alija was not saying a word like they have smelled the rat and Momo did not want to tell him why it would be to our benefit."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any discrepancies between the spoken B/C/S and what was listened by the interpreter's booth?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: None between the transcript and the English translation; however, the spoken words were too fast; it couldn't be matched.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any need for them to be replayed or is the Defence sufficiently ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Ms. Cmeric says there's a couple of things she can check, but she can do that later without taking the Court's time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelobrk, one of the things you mentioned before was following the federal constitution rather than the republican constitution. In the beginning, there seemed to be a discussion about that. Is that the matter that you were talking about?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That is one of the examples of the kind of thing I meant. The person who is mentioned here as Doko was the minister of defence. The government wanted to take additional measures in order to resolve the situation concerning weapons in Bosnia-Herzegovina, by managing these resources directly. There was an important need for taking such a measure, because there was a tangible threat of use of arms. It is obvious from the transcript that the SDA position is that the federal law should be applied, first and foremost, and then, number 2, that the municipalities would not obey the government, as mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelobrk, I'm looking at the transcript, and it comes off as your answer was: "It was obvious from the transcript that the SDA position is that the federal law should be applied." Did you mean to say SDA?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a slip. The SDS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in your statement, where you talk in paragraphs 26 and 27 about the parallel process, you also talked about regionalisation, which I think is what you referred to in an earlier answer in talking about the creation of the Serb autonomous regions. Do you recall when that first became public knowledge or in the awareness of the public, that there was any kind of formal media announcement about those Serb autonomous regions?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The public was formally informed only at the moment when these forms of regionalisation, as they termed them in the SDS, were formally established. The second aspect of it is that many of these notions did emerge in the press, in the independent media. Therefore, my direct answer to your question would be the following: There were no official, formal announcements of these acts, but by interpreting the different discussions that went on between various politicians, like, for instance, something that we heard in the penultimate transcript, and of course, this reached the Assembly members and we could infer our own conclusions. Thirdly, I was born and I live in Sarajevo; however, many of my colleagues live in other areas of Bosnia and Herzegovina. They directly conveyed to me the information as to what was going on in their communities. That was sufficient information for me, to be indirectly informed about all these processes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time I'd like to have the next CD given an exhibit number. And again, I have a single --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The next number is P399. The original B/C/S version transcript is P399A, and the English is P399A.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: For the booth, this excerpt starts about the middle of page 3 in the English and a third of the way down on page 2 of the B/C/S. It's about a minute and a half

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Momcilo KRAJISNIK: I spoke to Alija. Radovan KARADZIC: Yes. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Concerning the platform. Radovan KARADZIC: Yes. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: He says: You know, I have to think about it, I have to, because it's not concrete enough, you know. Radovan KARADZIC: Right. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Let me see, I think that Ganic agrees with it also, I have to see, so he stayed, but postponed it for Monday. Radovan KARADZIC: Uh-huh. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: But Nikola is now completely depressed. Radovan KARADZIC: Really? Momcilo KRAJISNIK: You know he gets all on fire but yesterday he was all, you know, I guess they didn't talk about it so it all seemed strange to him. Radovan KARADZIC: Uh-huh. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: I just told him, wait a minute, Nikola, understand, if he thought so, and if he didn't think so, he was not supposed to tell the gathering yesterday so publicly and we're not interested in him. As soon as we speak to them we'll sort it out ourselves. Come on. Radovan KARADZIC: Yes, yes. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: I told him not to get so upset over it, so he calmed down a little. This morning he came to me. Radovan KARADZIC: Yes, yes. We will face them with an alternative. We can do it this way. But you know what comes then. We are going to the national equality council. Nothing will come out of that and your Assembly can, can dissolve or, or return it to the previous state so that the Serbs can participate in it. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Yeah, well, I don't think at all. We will simply -- our project in the future when we spoke to him we'll go publicly with regionalisation because we'll say we've spoken to you, what do you want? Radovan KARADZIC: Yes, yes, right. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Over there we have nothing else our great problem is that -- Radovan KARADZIC: That's right, I have a newspaper here. We will release a little of it. A part. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Yeah. Radovan KARADZIC: In the public, so then -- Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Listen here: At 4.00 that guy Milojevic will come here and Miskin will come, Dokinic will come. So I'll have a look then regarding, you know, that map we spoke about. Radovan KARADZIC: Yeah, yeah. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: And then the two of us will have a look at it together and then at 6.00 we will go down there. There is some -- that thing, what's it called, the Executive Board, is it? Radovan KARADZIC: The executive is at six, is it? Momcilo KRAJISNIK: At six."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelobrk, my first question is: Can you tell us what the national equality council was?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a body which purported to discuss those issues that the politicians deemed relevant and important for national equality, for ethnic equality. This was a novelty in the state infrastructure, because I want to correct something I stated yesterday. The Presidency at the time had seven members, two from the ranks of the Serbs, two from the ranks of Croats, two from the ranks of Bosniaks, and one from the ranks of "others," and that institution itself had already had the competence, the authority to discuss issues related to ethnic equality. In any case, the Assembly had the competence to discuss these matters. In my opinion, this idea of creating this exclusive body was simply a way of trying to discuss Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the matters of ethnic equality in a narrow -- among a narrow circle of people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And by whom was this body created, and what authority or power did it have, if any?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall precisely what sort of an act it was, establishing the body, but it was an advisory body.
