All the positions presented from that body had to be decided upon ultimately, either by the Assembly or by the Presidency. But if I may, I would like to state the following: I mentioned yesterday that one of the key characteristics of such a practice was the choice of a defensive tactics. In that context, when it came to raising any issues within the ethnic equality council, it could have been decided upon in an exclusive matter. I will try to put it simply. The SDS platform text, at least one of its initial versions, insisted on the principle of regionalisation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which meant that every national government would basically exert its authority over a given territory of the country. But this was placed in a very exclusive way, that is to say, in an ultimatum type way: Either it is going to be this way or it is not going to be in any of these ways. And in this transcript, you can read such a statement, that regionalisation will be insisted upon regardless of what these institutions may decide upon. The times that lay ahead only served to confirm that choice of proceeding.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1991, when regionalisation became public, when some of the Serb Autonomous Regions were pronounced or announced, was there public discussion about it or discussion about this in the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it came to the decision-making process of -- or presenting any sort of a platform to the Assembly, nothing of that sort ever took place. However, from what the SDS MPs were saying, one could discern the inevitability of it actually happening, taking place, regardless of what the other MPs in the Assembly thought about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to move to another topic now, and this is in paragraph 54 of your statement. You refer to Mr. Krajisnik as being "moderate in his public statements." Can you tell the Judges what you meant by the use of that term "moderate." Compared to whom or compared to what?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, the terms he used in his public statements were far more tolerant and carefully chosen than the ones that we could see in the transcript and what we would actually conclude on the basis of the transcript. The way in which he was chairing the Assembly's sessions also seemed to point to a person that really wanted to abide by the democratic procedure and end the process in a tolerant way. Outside these official meetings, I had the occasion of experiencing his more fierce statements, even at an earlier stage. And in my statement, I did mention several such examples. I think it was in one of the interviews immediately before -- or actually, in the beginning of 1992, where Mr. Krajisnik gave a very clear public statement that was bordering on the statements contained in the transcript, and that the public did not have the opportunity of hearing before. I have to admit that, especially in summer and in autumn, he did gain a lot of sympathy, support, from the Croat and Bosniak public.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement, you did, and I think you just now said, that you had occasion or opportunity to see Mr. Krajisnik in a non-public setting, where his demeanour and choice of language was different. Can you give the Court some details about that, when that was, what the nature of those discussions were, and how that difference manifested itself.

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will describe a meeting that we had together. That year I was president of the trade union organisation in Sarajevo that had 220.000 members. There had been many strikes. One strike that was held in a large company in Sarajevo had as its objective the settlement of the debt of some 50 million dollars of a commercial company dealing with the trade in arms. Together with those who were holding the strike, we were asking for the, of course, company to intervene, but also for the government and the Assembly to intervene in the matter. Because it was clear that the organs of the federal government also had to be involved in the resolution of the problem. And the situation, which was very tense, I had a negotiating team that met with Mr. Krajisnik, but this meeting very soon got into quite different waters, far away from what actually the motives of those who had been holding the strike were. I recall that two questions were put to us: Was this something that was directed against the Serbs? And: Is there someone from among us who dislikes Belgrade? I will just say that the end of the whole matter was that, that same evening, the funds were deposited to the account of that company towards the debt. When I had the opportunity of working with Mr. Krajisnik, either on some commissions or other bodies, he was much more effusive than when seated at the chairman's seat of the Assembly. When I talked to other members of the SDS and listened to their very tough statements, I asked them whether other SDS leaders were of the same opinion that they held, and they always confirmed to me with absolute certainty that Mr. Krajisnik was of the same position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just intervene with one question. Could you give us a few examples of the -- I mean, you are qualifying the language used by Mr. Krajisnik, but could you give us examples, apart from the two you mentioned, whether it was against Serbs and whether some people didn't like Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the debates in the autumn of 1991, I could hear from Mr. Krajisnik in the discussions that we had during the sessions of the Assembly, I could hear him persuading me that basically there was no way that we could agree upon anything with the Muslims and that Bosnia and Herzegovina had to be divided. In my statement, I also mentioned a conversation that took place at his invitation. He invited Miro Lazovic, the then-head of the SDP club and my own boss, and the motive was the meeting of the Serbian intellectuals that was taking place at the time. The topic was: Why did we not support the SDS? The two of us were telling him that we looked upon Bosnia-Herzegovina as a country of citizens, and he was persuading us, trying to persuade us, that Bosnia and Herzegovina had to be divided along ethnic lines. I remember very well the last message he conveyed to us, and I quoted that one. That type of a country you're advocating won't exist in 200 years' time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I was still -- it was still on my mind that your testimony was about that meeting you had in your capacity as a trade union leader, about the debt that still had to be paid. What kind of language did he use in that meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That meeting didn't last very long, because the tensions heightened very soon. And instead of discussing how this whole operation of the settling the debt of that company could be brought about, there were these two questions that I mentioned, and workers who were there with me reacted strongly to that, and our conversation didn't last very long after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but in your statement it says, "he was passionately discussing with us." Were these the two questions? I could read it to you: "As a representative of the unions, I met with Krajisnik in his capacity as president of the Assembly, on one occasion. It was a meeting without media and he was passionately discussing with us. Our dialogue bordered on an open fight." Is that the meeting? Because that's the meeting described in paragraph 54. So I'd like to know exactly apart from the two examples you gave, what was the -- what were the words used during this passionate discussing and how did the dialogue border on an open fight?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I was facing an angry man, and I could not persuade him to try and discuss the actual problem that existed in the company.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My question was what words Mr. Krajisnik used which made you conclude that he was angry or passionately discussing or that your dialogue bordered on an open fight.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I usually measure anger in decibels, and I do remember it as being a very loud discussion. I have tried to quote, and I have quoted two statements. The rest was just the debate amongst a crowd of people, and I'm not really sure that I would be able to quote precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then my next question: How was the aspect of being pro- or anti-Serb involved in this? Was the debt owed by a private company owned by Serbs or was it -- I mean, how do you -- how did you understand these remarks by Mr. Krajisnik, whether this was against Serbs or whether this was -- or whether anyone didn't like Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, it was a state-owned company. Second, the money that was due, and I will now try to use the, so to say, spatial terminology, the money belonged to Sarajevo but was at the time in Belgrade. And of course, our demands were justified, and that was proved by the fact that the federal government sent the money to be deposited to that company's account that same evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So I do understand that the issue was that the money had to come from Belgrade and had to be paid to Sarajevo. And was it 50 million or 15 million? I did not clearly understand that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm speaking of my memory now, because of course this can be found in the record, but I think it was somewhere around 50 million dollars.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 50, 5-0. Yes. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you told us Mr. Krajisnik was already president of the Assembly at that time. Do you remember approximately when that was, what year and month?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was certainly in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The month could have been September, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to mark the next CD and give it an exhibit number. And I have one segment to play from here, but it's a long one. It's almost five minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, that would be number --?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be number P400. And the original B/C/S transcript is P400A, and the English translation is P400A.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: For the booths, this starts on page 2 of the English, about five lines down and the B/C/S is on the second page, ERN 95 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Momcilo KRAJISNIK: A Presidency meeting was held today, you know. Radovan KARADZIC: Uh-huh. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Well, they adopted some decisions. I don't know. I think that our lot did not understand it well. I looked at that platform. Radovan KARADZIC: Hmm. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: I think that it's not good. Radovan KARADZIC: Did they -- our lot did -- Momcilo KRAJISNIK: I don't know what they were doing. I think they did not rise to the occasion. They did not understand it. I don't know what we're going to do. Radovan KARADZIC: Hmm. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Believe me, according to the platform Bosnia and Herzegovina is a sovereign country. I'm afraid that's going to cause a scandal and there's going to be trouble. There's no Yugoslavia. It's two, three, or five times worse than anything that's been offered so far. Radovan KARADZIC: Well, never mind. They'll have a breakup of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Let me tell you something, to avoid participating in the breakup because it's wrong, we're not interested in that. I think a good thing to do would be, so to speak, to consult the two of ours. I don't know what they adopted. Radovan KARADZIC: Hmm. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: I think that is -- Radovan KARADZIC: Ours did -- Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Huh. Radovan KARADZIC: Ours gave a special, special, special -- Momcilo KRAJISNIK: I was here with a man who was present here. Radovan KARADZIC: Yeah, and what did he say? Momcilo KRAJISNIK: I think they did not understand each other. They did not understand what they want. The Presidency discussion has finished he thinks that we should - verb missing - him to finish. Radovan KARADZIC: Yes, the Presidency discussion has finished. Now it's the Assembly's turn, right? Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Yes. That wouldn't be -- I think that wasn't okay. I'm afraid there's going to be trouble in Bosnia-Herzegovina. We'll -- Radovan KARADZIC: They want it for the constitutional commission, don't they? Momcilo KRAJISNIK: No, no. It is for the Assembly. Radovan KARADZIC: How come? Well, it has to be for the constitutional commission. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Well, you see, there are two problems here. It was said that the platform was going to be for the Assembly but the problem is who does it go to for further procedure. Radovan KARADZIC: Uh-huh. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: You know that's it. Radovan KARADZIC: Uh-huh. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Because now they want it to have a non-constitutional character and it hasn't got a constitutional character, you know. Radovan KARADZIC: Yes. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: In this way, they have two documents. One for drawing up the constitution. Today I was so angry. Believe me, I haven't been angry for a long time. We have groups, you see, in the constitutional commission. Radovan KARADZIC: Yes. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Which constitute different, so to speak, fractions. And international relations. And I was supposed to do it. I said: Don't make me choose Miljanovic, that Gasa. He is a professor. He's realistic. Well, he's not much of a Serb, but it doesn't matter. Radovan KARADZIC: Uh-huh. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: He will know what should be done. Radovan KARADZIC: Yes. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Milan was supposed to go with him. Radovan KARADZIC: Uh-huh. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: And that Krstan Malesevic was appointed on behalf of the SDP. Radovan KARADZIC: Yes, yes. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: And a member of the government was suggested -- Radovan KARADZIC: Uh-huh. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: And a member of the Presidency. Two members, one of the government and the other of the Presidency. It has to be one of each of the three nationalities. And today I received the act -- Radovan KARADZIC: Uh-huh. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Finished. It's a real wonder. Radovan KARADZIC: None of our people were absent, right? Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Milan Trbojevic was also present and then I called. Ranko was there for 15 minutes. Micic was there but he had no authorisation. Well, that Mijanovic was absent. Krstan was absent. And, get this, it -- I think of Serbs -- what was -- because that's what we had agreed at the national composition. Milan Trbojevic was present. He came to me and said, get this, we have agreed to - verb missing - now. There were all sorts of remarks, that somebody should summarise it and then we should sit down again. Radovan KARADZIC: Yes. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: And they draft it. It's finished, and they send it to the representatives and members of the constitutional commission, to other commissions to deal with. Radovan KARADZIC: You know what you should do. Have Milan Trbojevic write it for you, an official letter to. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: All right. I know what I've done. Everything -- they have -- I said you have to be responsible to the people. Are you passing on what the interests of the people are? And he will write it down. Because that's really a mistake of this Cazim Sadikovic. Radovan KARADZIC: Yes. Yes. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: But it's not possible, man, on that people everyone is taking away. There's no one there. It's a total chaos. Well, I said, well, do you understand man, I'm not -- you will start a revolution, you, man -- first, I don't think that we should now act to the benefit of the Serbs. But, man, you can't do it that way. People will spit on you. And they will make us traitors. Radovan KARADZIC: How did Trbojevic behave then? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Well, how. Radovan KARADZIC: He doesn't see the danger, does he? Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Well, that's the problem, I think. It's hard for me to say this. To hell with silky and Ranko. I was there for 15 minutes. I had no authorisation. Oh, Simovic sent Ranko, Ranko said since I didn't go, I left the place later they can go to -- Radovan KARADZIC: Well, you should engage Simovic. You should leave out Ranko a bit. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Well, I told them today, for God's sake, people -- I was so angry. Well, it is clear to you, man, what -- do you understand that this is not -- you have no right to pass on that information. Where's your alternative, if nothing else. How can you do that? They say, well, it's not -- well, then you know they start well, we added it. Well, you can add it. You know what, you have what -- Radovan KARADZIC: They will not let the bill to be passed. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Well, no -- we are -- Radovan KARADZIC: That's their -- Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Well, we have clearly defined what it is. And you can pass what it is, man, people want -- and not what you think or what you think somebody else would think. This is an amendment to the act where we have to say precisely some want this, others that, and let the people decide. Radovan KARADZIC: Yes, yes. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: And the Assembly, three -- two thirds or one third majority, one third. You can't use tactics, half of this, half of that. But you have to tell me precisely, please, the alternative is -- federative Yugoslavia and federal units. Bosnia is a sovereign, an equal and sovereign state and let them decide who wants what. Radovan KARADZIC: Yes. Yes."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelobrk --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No discrepancies noticed that need any further attention.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: To the extent the interpreters could follow, none.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelobrk, this intercept is dated, I believe, the 14th of August, 1991, although --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do we find that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It does not appear on my copy of the transcript. I will ask you:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware of discussions about the platform being discussed in the late summer/early fall in the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One of the conclusions of the Assembly, in view of various memorandums or resolutions of different authors and different political parties, was to bring all of this together through a single platform which would initially be drafted by the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So this comment has to do with that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that matter was also being discussed in the Presidency, as well as in the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. So the Presidency discussed it for two reasons. First of all, because this had to do with the general situation and the Presidency is responsible for the general situation in the country. And when preparing all sessions of the presidents of the republics, the Presidency would formulate its own positions. So when this one member of the Presidency went to represent them there, he or she would have their positions. It is the Assembly also that was in charge of such matters, and therefore, the Presidency followed what was going on in the Assembly and what was said in the parliamentary debates. At the end of July 1991 and the beginning of August 1991, efforts were made by the Presidency to work out this single document that would be verified by the Presidency itself and the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I want to go into the October 8th session of the Assembly. That's a new topic. Would this be an appropriate time for the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it would be, Mr. Hannis. I make one observation. The suggestion made by both parties might result in having to send back two witnesses home and to call them back. The Chamber will consider over the next break whether it still supports that suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, in connection with that, may I advise you of one matter. We had some discussion with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps we first ask Madam Usher to escort the witness out of the courtroom. We'll have a break, Mr. Bjelobrk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we appreciate the share the Court's concerns about that possibility and we did discussion that with Mr. Stewart, Mr. Harmon and myself during the last break, and we thought about what would be the possibility if we sent Mr. Bjelobrk home and started with Witness 629 tomorrow, with the possibility that we might be able to finish him, since he's only here for cross-examination. However, he did testify for approximately five days in Brdjanin. It was an extensive examination. There were, I believe, about 70 exhibits shown to him at that time. I've spoken with Mr. Harmon, and he's not sure that, depending on how long the cross-examination was, how much redirect there would be, and given the number of exhibits, we might still have to send him home as well. That's why we proposed the other procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for this additional information. We'll consider the matter and we'll have a break until 10 minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, would you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I inquire if the Court decided which procedure --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber has again considered whether it would prefer to hear Witness 629 or Mr. Bjelobrk -- the start of the cross-examination of Mr. Bjelobrk. And the Chamber decided that we would continue in the way we intended to go. That means that we start the cross-examination of Mr. Bjelobrk tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelobrk, now I'd like to take you to October 10th, 11th, and 14th of 1991, the 8th Session of the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And you talk about this in your statement in paragraphs 40 to 42, paragraph 46, and paragraphs 49 and 50. Just briefly, concisely, can you tell us what was the topic that caused such heated debate at this session and eventually led to the SDS walking out? What was the main topic on the agenda that led to that result?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The main item on the agenda was the position of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the Yugoslav crisis. The underlying idea at that session was to try to come to a document, yet again, which would establish the positions of the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina in relation to the crisis. The session had two parts. The first part of the session was marked by a very broad debate, and then an attempt was made to draft a document which was supposed to be conducive to the second part of the parliamentary debate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were there various documents relating to that issue proposed by more than one party?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Formally speaking, there were several proposals, but the discussion made it obvious that the previously formulated proposals would be put forth too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you briefly three short questions. Was there an SDS proposal on the agenda?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, they had a proposal of their own too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there an SDA memorandum?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your party, the SDP, had a proposal as well?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We kept bringing up the proposal we drafted during the summer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in your statement, you talk about the speech that Mr. Karadzic made at one point, and it's also in the record that you spoke on that occasion. But there came a point in time where the SDS walked out and Mr. Krajisnik ended the session, as president of the Assembly, he ended the session; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, the last three speakers during that part of the session were yours truly, Mr. Karadzic, and Mr. Izetbegovic. After that, there was a break, and after the break, the Assembly was adjourned. In my opinion, and that was the general feeling, it happened very abruptly and unexpectedly. Afterwards, a rule was found in the rules of procedure that the vice-president could chair the remainder of the session, even in the absence of the SDS MPs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in the absence of the SDS representatives, were there still enough representatives to compose a quorum in terms of numbers?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a quorum, but there was this doubt concerning the quorum that had been raised earlier on as to whether the representatives of the three ethnic parties had to be there, regardless of that rule that was contained in the rules of procedure, exactly providing for the number of representatives that had to be present to compose a quorum.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I'd like to have the next document marked as an exhibit. It is -- well, let me ask you a question about marking this before we give it a number. This is the -- these are the minutes of the 8th Session on the 10th, 11th, and 14th of October, 1991. A document of that nature relating to those minutes is an exhibit to Mr. Treanor's expert report. It is in the binder 6 -- Exhibit 64A, and I believe it's at tab 435. However, I wasn't able to ascertain whether the version that is in that binder is the full minutes or -- there is a translation that only has highlighted portions. So I don't know if you want me to use that same number, and we have a copy --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If it's the -- if it is the same document, so if you say I don't remember, you will understand that I could not answer that question by heart, whether that was the full or the -- but perhaps you could check. No. I think even that it might not be in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No. Because the footnotes are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll not assign a number to it yet. You're invited to check overnight whether it's exactly the same document. If not, then it will be given a number tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That will work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelobrk, did you have an opportunity to review that document before testifying today?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recognise it as reflecting the minutes of what happened during that session of the BH Assembly?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are the official minutes of that particular session of the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Before we continue, Mr. Hannis, we have heard some observations made by Mr. Krajisnik on what are correct text or not. I'd like to ask Mr. Krajisnik at this moment, although not as a witness but as a defendant, whether there's any alternative version of those minutes that he would like to put to the witness at a later stage so that we can already take that into account when listening to the witness. Is there an alternative version?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is the short version, the minutes that I was referring to, and here we have the stenographic notes, which is much larger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand. Mr. Hannis, you are not aware of the content of these stenographic notes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm not, Your Honour. I can't frankly tell you whether we have those stenographic notes for this session of the BiH Assembly or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just ask whether Mr. Krajisnik would allow the Chamber just to have a glance at the stenographic notes so that we have any idea about the size of it. But, of course, only -- I would say -- Mr. Krajisnik, I take it that you have consulted Mr. Stewart on this, or at least discussed it with Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we can tell Your Honours that the notes for the 14th of October, and of course there are all those previous days, constitute just about a hundred pages, 98 pages, something like that. That's for the 14th, that one day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could I just have a brief look at it, just to get an impression on what it looks like.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to at least allow Mr. Hannis to have a glance on it. If there would be any issue raised in a question which would look quite different if one would consult the stenographic notes or if there's really -- it's a wrong representation or a misleading presentation of what has been said, then the Chamber exceptionally would like to be informed about that. And whether this is done by the accused himself, by Mr. Krajisnik himself, or through you, I leave that up to, well, policy to be developed by the Defence. But we'd rather not spend a lot of questions and time on an issue where the basis could be subject to serious doubt because the minutes would reflect not what has been said. At least the Chamber would like to be informed about it. So, therefore, it's not necessary to intervene immediately, if a question is put, but we would like to avoid that we'd hear questions and answers for 15 or 20 minutes on a subject which would look totally different if you would look at the stenographic notes. This is not to say that the Chamber, by giving such an opportunity, accepts the authenticity of the stenographic notes. Nothing is said about that. It's just a very practical approach of the matter at this very moment. And perhaps I also should then perhaps remind the parties, both Prosecution and Defence, that of course the way in which political parties have developed and formulated their goals, what strategies or others would call it perhaps games or tricks be played in order to get that -- to achieve aims and goals is not the core of this case. I'm not saying that political matters are insignificant for this case, but that's not the core of this case. And I'd like to remind the parties of that. So, therefore, even if this Chamber is confronted with, in statements or testimonies about political analysis of a certain situation, the most important thing, then, for the Chamber is that in evidence is that someone analysed the political situation in that way, and not necessarily that such an analysis makes any sense at all. I'm not saying that it makes sense, does not make sense, but if not a proper, factual foundation for such analysis is given, it's just the analysis, it's just the opinion of a person. The Chamber -- you may have noticed that some questions were put to this witness to -- of course, not to demonstrate, because that was not the purpose, but that could demonstrate the approach of this Chamber, that is, analysis, qualifications, are of minor assistance to the Chamber, whereas facts are the most important things this Chamber will look at. Please proceed, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I just ask: I happen to know, as Mr. Hannis knows, in my case, that it's unlikely, with respect, that Mr. Hannis's grasp of B/C/S will enable him to do a deep analysis of the document in his hands at the moment. But since it is Mr. Krajisnik's document and since it does have, I think, some of his notes, I wonder, when a glance --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's already back. I'm so sorry. Things happen when you're not looking and it's already back. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps it's even difficult for you to follow the course of a B/C/S document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm acknowledging. We know each other's limitations as far as that goes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And actually, I'm intending to ask the witness about events that happened after Mr. Krajisnik left and I think the stenographic minutes he has don't cover the period that I'm going to go into now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand that it's the 14th of October. So if we come to that, it makes any sense if we are still at the 10th or the 11th, it's different. Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelobrk, after the SDS had walked out and Mr. Krajisnik had adjourned the session, I understand that those of you who remained were enough to constitute a quorum. Is that correct? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was enough of us to constitute a quorum.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after consulting the rules and having some discussion, did you continue to have a session in the absence of the SDS and Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The vice-president of the Assembly, Mariofil Ljubic continued to chair the session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you conduct some business during that session, vote on some of the proposals?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Assembly discussed and adopted a memorandum containing several paragraphs that were determining the position of Bosnia and Herzegovina in respect of the Yugoslav crisis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the details --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the details of that are reflected in the minutes before you as to which items were voted on and whether they passed?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you waiting for my answer?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. The substance is contained in the minutes, and in my statement, I presented paragraphs 1 to 3, and I analysed in some detail paragraph 6, which insisted on the use of political means only for the resolution of the crisis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that memorandum also expressed the principle that you mentioned earlier in your testimony about Bosnia maintaining equidistance between itself and Croatia, on the one hand, and Serbia on the other; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. That constituted the minimum from which we would not depart in terms of our position for the resolution of the Yugoslav crisis, that equidistance in relation to Serbia and Croatia, and internally the equality of every single citizen and nation constituting the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I underline that the sixth item was a novelty for the Assembly. It was drafted in response to Mr. Karadzic's address, that the only means for the resolution of crisis allowed are going to be the political ones.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: And democratic ones.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. After this session ended, then, was there a reaction or a position that the SDS took in response to your -- I mean the remaining delegates who stayed after the SDS walkout, was there an SDS response to the actions that you all had taken in that post-walkout session?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The basic message from the SDS was that the Assembly could not adopt anything without consulting the will of one nation, and I've almost quoted their position here. But they were not familiar with either the text of the document or the way in which it was adopted. A combination of facts that occurred later on proved to be the radicalisation of their position in terms of their creating an Assembly of the Serbian People.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, next I would like to have a CD, another intercept, given the next number and played to this witness. There's only one segment from this intercept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The next number is P401; the B/C/S transcript is 401A; and English translation 401A.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, before we begin, for the interpreters, the English begins about the middle of page 5 and the B/C/S begins at the bottom of page ERN 03236578. And during proofing, the witness pointed out to me, in listening to the conversation, that there appeared to be a word that he heard spoken that did not appear in the B/C/S transcript. I spoke about that with Ms. Cmeric. She heard the same missing word. It is in the B/C/S about halfway down on page 6579, where Mr. Karadzic is speaking. In the English, it is on page 6, at the top, the second box, where Mr. Karadzic is speaking, the word missing appears to be "ne," in the context meaning not, and I would ask if the interpreters could listen carefully for that where Mr. Karadzic is speaking about what Alija said about controlling the entire Bosnia and whether they hear the same thing that the witness and Ms. Cmeric have heard. And with that, I'm ready to begin playing, if everyone else is ready.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Djogo GOJKO: And you must bust this, man, this -- I mean, before everybody, that, that representative of yours, Bogicevic. Radovan KARADZIC: Yes. No, on the next Assembly session we shall ask from him to resign. Although everybody denied him trust, he has to resign. And finally they have to work, no matter how many of them are there. They must work. I don't know -- not Mesic. Mesic is a traitor. He betrayed his oath and the fact that he doesn't want it, doesn't oblige us to anything. If he doesn't want it, it doesn't mean that Yugoslavia doesn't exist. Djogo GOJKO: Yes. Yes. Radovan KARADZIC: That means that he betrayed that Yugoslavia. So, they should work. They must work. The government and the Assembly and everything. And now, from here, we shall make them work. You know? Djogo GOJKO: That should be -- I don't know how the Muslims will take it. You know. They might, you know, start something somewhere or start some kind of negotiations you know or maybe simply take over. Radovan KARADZIC: Here -- no -- Djogo GOJKO: Some of the territories, you know. Radovan KARADZIC: No. No negotiation. Because Alija they will probably ask for -- want to accept what we did and they'll want to mark their territory as well, and that will be the end of it. Djogo GOJKO: Muslims, huh? Radovan KARADZIC: Yes, I believe in that. Because Alija said, if we cannot control the entire Bosnia, then we'll choose what we can control with success, take over with success. Djogo GOJKO: Uh-huh. Radovan KARADZIC: Because he really wants to achieve that Islamic way of life of his and we have nothing against it. Djogo GOJKO: Yes. Yes. Radovan KARADZIC: But it's no good. He's been thought not to like the state and that's it. Djogo GOJKO: Well, what can you do? You can agree on what you will control. Radovan KARADZIC: Well, right. There are those Muslim areas and so on. We can agree on all of that nothing is -- Djogo GOJKO: Yes. Yes. Radovan KARADZIC: Nothing is -- impossible. Djogo GOJKO: Uh-huh. Radovan KARADZIC: But in any case, there's no special agreement because we are discussing this for three months now and then they can pull this thing with memorandum. Djogo GOJKO: Yes. Radovan KARADZIC: And adopt it in an unconstitutional manner. I don't want to discuss anything anymore. Djogo GOJKO: Well, that's like -- you give him a hand and he, you know -- Radovan KARADZIC: No, he thinks you are weak, weak because you are kind. Djogo GOJKO: Yes, yes. Radovan KARADZIC: We are not weak now. We have -- Djogo GOJKO: Uh-huh. Radovan KARADZIC: -- entire Serbian people. More than we had for the elections, man. And more, it's such a force that is behind us now."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, Mr. Hannis, does the word appear in the translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The word does not appear in the translation, nor does it appear in the transcript of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Are you going to provide a new version of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, assuming that we're all in agreement, I propose to provide a corrected B/C/S transcript and an English translation, including that word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's right. And then just for my better understanding: How would then the translation read on the relevant part?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe it would say -- do you want to ask me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, at least -- but if Ms. Cmeric would help us out, but then not for the B/C/S but... If you read perhaps the line where the word "ne" appears then we hear from the translator how the translation should be.

utterances.speaker: MS. CMERIC
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. "Radovan KARADZIC: Yes, I believe in that, because Alija said that if we cannot control the entire Bosnia, then we'll choose what we can control successfully, that is, gain."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, where does the negative miss in the translation, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe not --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I believe the word "not" needs to be inserted between can and control on the first line of what Mr. Karadzic is saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I read in my translation "cannot."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. Perhaps I have a copy that does not include it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And could we just look, since there seem to be different versions, and I'll see whether the B/C/S really is not the right one. Let me just have a look. Ms. Cmeric, could you -- I think that in the B/C/S version, we are in the middle of page 6579, last four digits.

utterances.speaker: MS. CMERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we are in the box where Mr. Karadzic, Radovan, starts saying "Da" and then [B/C/S spoken] or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CMERIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then where would the -- where's the word missing?

utterances.speaker: MS. CMERIC
utterances.text: It's missing in the next sentence [B/C/S spoken] and then the word after "Ako," between words "Ako" and "Budemo". It has to be "Ako ne Budemo".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So what I understand is that the translation is not correct to the extent that it includes the word "cannot," but if we would add "ne" in this part then the translation would be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. It appears that I have an earlier copy of the English translation without the "not" in it. You have a copy with "not" in it, but we both have the B/C/S version with no ne.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's a bit confusing that the translation is corrected, and not the original. But it's clear now. So we only get a new copy of the B/C/S version and not of the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, while we were on that little box, apart from the obvious typo of then instead of than in the English, which is fairly clear, I think, we had -- or Ms. Cmeric, I should say, that's the "we" had a slight problem with the last line there, where the English translation at the moment says "takeover with success" which wasn't what came across from the interpreters and it's not what came across to me from Ms. Cmeric either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me first ask the interpreters: Were you able to follow the B/C/S text and was the transcript in B/C/S correct or not?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We tried, Your Honour. It was very fast, and we tried to do our best. We think it is all there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You think it's all there. So of course, Ms. Cmeric, if there would be any need ... And then is it a matter of translation, Ms. Cmeric, or is it a matter of incorrect transcribing the B/C/S text?

utterances.speaker: MS. CMERIC
utterances.text: It is a matter of translation, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you then please read, slowly, the relevant part so that the interpreters could assist us in providing us with the English version.

utterances.speaker: MS. CMERIC
utterances.text: Yes. It is in fact the same part, Your Honour. It's just -- the same box. It's just the end of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please slowly read that. So perhaps from then we'll choose. Is it the last part? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CMERIC
utterances.text: Yes. [Interpretation] "Choose that which we can control successfully, or rather, gain."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the difference in the translation is now that the word "gain" is used rather than "takeover."

utterances.speaker: MS. CMERIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we take that -- I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I was just commenting to Ms. Cmeric and also that the with success is not repeated, as it is on the text we have. So that drops off the end. That's how I understood --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask the interpreters to confirm that the words "with success" are used only once in relation to control and not again used after the word "gain."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So, Mr. Hannis, I think that you've got now sufficient guidance to provide us both with the new B/C/S version and --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do not know whether it's really necessary to have it all copied again, because whatever should be changed, I changed in my copy, which of course is not the official copy. If the copy for the registrar is the finally --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think we can make those changes on the individual page and not have to change any of the rest and substitute that page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Unless the parties would agree that with my -- that I would change the copy that has handed now to the registrar. I mean, these are not originals.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're happy with that. And all this stuff is on the transcript as well, so we're perfectly happy with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then we'll change it by hand. I'll give it my - how do you call that?- my signature and then it's not necessary to copy some other 50 or 60 pages for that purpose. Please proceed, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, to clear up one remaining mystery as to why the word "ne" was not changed in the B/C/S translation, it's my understanding this was a B/C/S transcript that was provided to us by an outside agency and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mistake and there was no one who intentionally did it, but if so, that needs another investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelobrk, on that intercept that we just listened to, at the beginning, it talked about an individual named Bogicevic. Can you tell us who that was?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bogicevic was a member of the Presidency of Yugoslavia at the time. He was elected in Bosnia and Herzegovina and represented Bosnia and Herzegovina in that body. Otherwise, he was a member and one of the leaders of the Social Democratic Party. He was known for having opposed the logic that stood behind the events leading up to the Yugoslav crisis, and since he is a Serb by ethnicity, he was criticised by all those who thought that he did not advocate the Serb positions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in that intercept, Mr. Karadzic indicates that at the next Assembly session, they will ask him to resign. Do you know if there was a call for him to resign sometime after this November 11th conversation?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout the year, criticism was levelled at him for his representation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and if I recall well, in November, at one of the Assembly sessions, he submitted a report on his work, and there were differing opinions, of course, as to the quality of his work. If you allow me to remind you, the recordings and the transcripts of the session of the Yugoslav Presidency on the key issues have now been made public. He directly opposed the introduction of military measures in Yugoslavia, in such a way that he opposed those people who represented the Serb positions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You heard where Mr. Karadzic talked about them pulling this thing with the memorandum and adopting it in an unconstitutional manner. Do those remarks reflect the SDS position about the memorandum that you all had passed in the post-walkout session?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I've understood you correctly, he -- if I understood it correctly, he said that the document had been adopted in a manner that was not in accordance with the procedure.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: That was illegitimate. Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the standard of legitimacy is the statute of the Assembly, then the document was passed in a legitimate way. If we, by legitimacy, mean the consensus by all three national parties, then such a conclusion would be justified and founded. But this was merely an agreement between the national -- three national parties as to what they thought was legitimate in the Assembly's proceedings. Perhaps I should not be the one to say Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. this, but Bosnia-Herzegovina was, under the constitution, defined as a state of its constitutive nations and citizens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Controversy over the legitimacy is well known to the Chamber. We had a lot of evidence and this Chamber does not pretend to be the constitutional court of either Bosnia-Herzegovina or one of the entities contained in it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelobrk, let me move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If the next item could be given an exhibit number. This is a newspaper article from Oslobodjenje, 1 January 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document will be marked P402.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I said 1 January. I see the English says 12 January. I'm looking at the original B/C/S, and perhaps I can get some help from Ms. Cmeric. Part of it looks like 31/12/1991. And then I don't know if it's 1 -- 1, 2 January 1992. I don't know what date that actually reflects it came out on.

utterances.speaker: MS. CMERIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Mr. Hannis is correct. The date is 31st of December, 1991, 1st and 2nd January, 1992. It's probably new year's eve issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's around new year.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelobrk, do you recall seeing this interview of Mr. Izetbegovic published in the newspaper about that time?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall this interview.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And without going into the details of what's in the interview, do you recall if he was talking about the idea of an independent Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He shared this idea too, of an independent, sovereign Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall, after this interview was given, hearing any reaction from SDS members or any particular SDS individuals talking about what he had said, Mr. Izetbegovic had said in his interview?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was one of the many such presentations, and it did not really constitute news from the point of view of the general public. I know that there were some sharp comments after the interview was published. I consider the interview of Mr. Krajisnik to be an important one, though one that was published also in January, 1992, right after this one. And on the basis of a similar structure, he presented the views of the party that he belonged to. In a way, it was a kind of response to Izetbegovic's interview, although I do not believe that it had that dimension only.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelobrk, I hope to get to that shortly. If I could now have the next CD marked as an exhibit. This is an intercept, Your Honour. I have three different segments in this one that I would like to play. They're all relatively short. I think the longest is a minute and a half. And the first one begins on the first page, in both the B/C/S and the English?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I do want to raise one point regarding the number. I understand that when Mr. Harmon presented a binder of intercepts to Mr. Kljuic, I believe it was 292. This -- the transcript of this intercept was marked with KID number 30911 in that binder, but the audio was not played for Mr. Kljuic. So I'm not sure how we should number this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, as a matter of fact, I would like to have the CD to be assigned a number and that a similar number with the A, B, and C, and the .1 assigned to these documents to avoid whatever confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The next number is P403.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And we have then now P403A as the first section to be played.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Did Nikola call you. Radovan KARADZIC: Yes. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: What do you think about that idea? Radovan KARADZIC: What idea? Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Did he tell you? Radovan KARADZIC: Nah. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: You can say -- you can tell he didn't tell me. He said -- he told the people from Banja Luka these people from Krajina, that is, it's terrible. Radovan KARADZIC: Oh, that. He did tell me that. You know what? The dislocation of this thing from Sarajevo is an idiotic idea. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Yes -- I don't know. Radovan KARADZIC: Never mind. Let me tell you, that is a very dangerous idea. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: You think? Radovan KARADZIC: Of course it is, man. It is so dangerous I forgot about it immediately. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Huh? Radovan KARADZIC: It is so dangerous I forgot about it immediately. Radovan KARADZIC: Well, I can tell you, I don't know, it all depends, you know what the most important thing is? The most important thing is that we've already held the first session of the parliament. The most important thing is that this session was held there. Radovan KARADZIC: I'm afraid that's already Momcilo KRAJISNIK: That's true. That's -- Radovan KARADZIC: Very dangerous. This battle needs to be won here, not there. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: You know what, I know that, but you know how it is when something is pronounced at a place where separatism -- then -- and you pronounce Sarajevo the capital. Radovan KARADZIC: All right. Maybe we should give it a thought. I'm not sure about -- Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Neither am I, neither am I. It's just that even if you have the worst idea if you turn it into something positive then it turns out to be great, you know. Radovan KARADZIC: Yes. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Because there is great separatism there, you know. Radovan KARADZIC: Yes. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: So it means a lot when you say this is the HQ here, you pronounce it the centre of everything and thus you keep it. This way, you turn this into a long-term thing, because they can't do anything else in a situation like this. Radovan KARADZIC: Yes, yes. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Every one of these things has its own significance. I've been thinking about this a long time and it's something -- fuck, I don't know. Radovan KARADZIC: We should think about it. I don't know. We should think about it."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No major discrepancies?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Not any major ones, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. In the interest of time, I'd like to move to the next clip, which begins on the bottom of page 4 in the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Here again ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Begins with Mr. Karadzic talking about reading the interview. And in the B/C/S, I believe that begins on page 5, or ERN 03220530.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Radovan KARADZIC: Fuck her, fuck her. I was just reading this Izetbegovic's interview. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Yeah. What's it's like? Radovan KARADZIC: Well, he's crazy, man. He -- he is directly irritating the Serbs. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Yeah? Radovan KARADZIC: He was like: If we're all the same, this and that, and a sovereign and independent Bosnia. Now he's talking openly of a sovereign and independent Bosnia. Does he want someone to destroy Sarajevo? Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Yeah. Radovan KARADZIC: Fuck, he's really crazy. He now openly talks of a sovereign and independent Bosnia. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Yeah. Radovan KARADZIC: You know, that -- Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Yeah. Radovan KARADZIC: It was until recently -- fuck him. We will release our tigers and let them do their job. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Yeah, can you imagine this impertinence. Radovan KARADZIC: Fuck, I've -- we've been calming the Serb people for a year because of his foolishness. What can I do? I will not be calming anyone any more, nor can I. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: No, but he says -- we don't want -- this isn't an independent -- that's not a state, he says, it's a sovereign -- so it is equal in the talks. Now he says independent, fucking -- they really are crazy. Europe is crazy too if they think this can be so. Man, this is impossible, this -- I don't think there's a man who would turn the situation around now and make it so. Radovan KARADZIC: No, no. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: No. These are -- man. Radovan KARADZIC: No way. We need to release those people. We shouldn't hold them back. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: We have to, but they'll do it anyway, whether you want them to or not. Radovan KARADZIC: Like I said, you can't hold them back any more."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No major discrepancies?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, then I would like to go to the last segment and the last intercept I intend to play. This is not marked on your copy, I believe, of the English, but it starts on page 6, a little over a third of the way down, where Mr. Karadzic begins by saying: "I don't know. Let him do whatever..." In the B/C/S, it's on page ERN 0322-0531, about halfway down the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then until where?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And then it goes until the bottom of page 6 in the English, the last line. And in the B/C/S, I believe it goes to about a third of the way down on page number 0532. Mr. Krajisnik is the last speaker.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover]. "Radovan KARADZIC: I don't know. Let me him do whatever he wants. I don't have anything against this. But we cannot hold our people back any more. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Yeah. He sent up a trial balloon. Today I heard on the radio he had said new currency was due. I was like fuck, man. Radovan KARADZIC: Yeah. He wants war. He is playing with fire, thinking Serbs wouldn't -- Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Yes. Radovan KARADZIC: He thinks Serbs wouldn't -- and he can't even introduce his currency in Pale, Novo Sarajevo. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: No way. Radovan KARADZIC: Let alone somewhere else. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Exactly. Radovan KARADZIC: He's also disseminated the idea that Serbs would be a minority in Sarajevo. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Yes. Radovan KARADZIC: You know, I mean, he is very unfair, and he's after irritating the Serbs to the maximum. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: We have to use the first opportunity to tell him that he's playing with fire. And we'll say clearly that they're playing with fire. Radovan KARADZIC: We will not tell him in private, but we shall do so in public, and him -- Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Yeah, in public. That's what I meant. Radovan KARADZIC: In private we'll tell him some other things. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Yes, yes, and that's clear."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did Your Honour wish to inquire if there were any discrepancies?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I should have asked. But I take it that if there would be major discrepancies, that the booth would warn me anyhow. But I should have asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the answer is, I take it, that there are no major discrepancies.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: No major, no, discrepancies.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, If we could mark -- give the next item a number. It's an interview of Mr. Krajisnik dated the 26th of January, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelobrk, would you take a look at that and tell us if that's the interview you referred to earlier in your testimony.

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the interview.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in your written statement that is in evidence in this case, at paragraph 55, I believe, you discuss that in some detail. And I don't have any other questions for you about that at the moment, but is there any comment you wanted to make, that you haven't, in connection with it?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since in paragraph 55, I have about seven sub-items and I stated my positions regarding the interview, perhaps I can reiterate only the following: There is a polemic going on, and the problem is not the fact that it is taking place, that is to say, what kind of statehood can Bosnia-Herzegovina achieve through all the stages of the crisis and the claims that it is impossible for Bosnia-Herzegovina to remain in a single state after disintegration, by introducing clauses of war, destruction, and the like. That is what astonished every normal person, that these categories should be used when assessing different views.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Finally, if the last item, a news article from Slobodna Bosna, could be given the next number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelobrk, we're about to hand you an item that, I believe, is what you referred to in your statement in paragraph 61. I want to ask you if you recall having seen this before.

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall having seen it before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this was published in March of 1992?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I comment. Mr. Krajisnik, surprise, surprise, is not able to read the B/C/S version, which is in such minuscule print on the photocopy that it would be a challenge to anybody. That's -- P402 is the same, same problem, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is true for P405 or -- because I have a large -- which --?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: 404 and -- well, 405 we've just got to. That doesn't -- no, 405 is not a problem, Your Honour. That's satisfyingly large. But it is really absolutely impossible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but which ones are the --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: 402 and 404, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that's a fair point. We will try to enlarge that and provide a larger copy, hopefully without losing any quality of the print.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because the quality seems already to be a bit ... But, well, since -- when do you think you could provide that? I mean, it's just making a 200-per-cent copy, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we could put it in their box at the front gate within the hour after we finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The problem is that Mr. Krajisnik would like to have it. I don't know how much time it would take before he -- and I don't know whether there are any rules that would prevent him from taking anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's not, I think, an insoluble problem here, because we're planning to see Mr. Krajisnik pretty early tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So if it would be in your box, then you could bring it to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, and he's got generally enough to do, Your Honour. I am concerned whether it is going to blow up, but then Mr. Hannis will do his best to see what we can do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thanks anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's try to get the best quality, and it will be within one hour in your box, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The last questions I have for you, Mr. Bjelobrk, relate to paragraph 32. You talk about some efforts by Serbs to try to get you to join them, and you name three individuals in paragraph 32: Mr. Knezevic, Mr. Bijelic, and Mr. Nedic. Who were they? Did they hold any position? Were they also members of the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The names that I mentioned in paragraph 32, namely, Savo Knezevic, Slobodan Bijelic, Miladin Nedic, are only a selection of people I talked to from the SDS, and this I brought to your attention as a common denominator. Basically, what they were saying was that all Serbs should live in one state and that they could not live together with other peoples, other nations. I would like to underline that I had similar conversations with Momcilo Krajisnik and Miro Lazovic, and I spoke of that too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, you did mention that earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, those are all the questions I have for Mr. Bjelobrk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Mr. Bjelobrk, it's 7.00, the time we usually finish. Mr. Hannis has concluded your examination-in-chief. We'll adjourn. We'd like to see you back tomorrow at a quarter past 2.00 in this same courtroom. May I instruct you not to speak with anyone about the testimony you have given and you're still about to give. Madam Usher, could you please escort Mr. Bjelobrk out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there are no procedural issues, then we adjourn. I again would like to remind the parties that this is not a constitutional court, this is not a court which finally deals with what are appropriate political means to achieve your goals or not, and also, I'd like to stress the relative importance of many such matters. And if you'd keep that in mind in your preparations for tomorrow, that would be highly appreciated. We adjourn until tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
